blocks.text: PROPHET; HIS BOOK NAMES NO KING · TWO KINGDOMS
Joel. He called Judah to fast after the locusts, and spoke of the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
“The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel.”
“The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel.” The book gives no date and no king. Joel 1:1
He calls the priests and the people to a fast and a solemn assembly in the house of the LORD. Joel 1:13–14 Joel 2:15–17
The word in its main themes
“Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation”
“for the day of the LORD is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?”
“And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God”
“And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten”
“I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy”
The nations in the valley of decision
“Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision”
To whom the word was spoken
“Gird yourselves, and lament, ye priests: howl, ye ministers of the altar”
“Yea, and what have ye to do with me, O Tyre, and Zidon, and all the coasts of Palestine?”
“Egypt shall be a desolation, and Edom shall be a desolate wilderness”
1 Locusts, drought, and the call to fast Joel 1:1–2:17
2 The LORD's answer: the years restored Joel 2:18–27
3 The Spirit poured out on all flesh Joel 2:28–32
4 The nations judged; Judah for ever Joel 3:1–21
WHERE THE NEW TESTAMENT QUOTES IT · 2
Each band joins a chapter of Joel to the New Testament books quoting it (2 books).
Who stood with him, and against him
From the textScripture says nothing of Joel beyond his father's name and his book. Joel 1:1
Early, before Amos (in the reign of Joash or soon after)
K. A. Credner (1831), as reported by Driver (1891); E. B. Pusey (1860); A. F. Kirkpatrick (1892, “on the whole”), as reported by G. A. Smith (1898)

Pusey reasons that Amos opens with Joel's words (“The LORD will roar from Zion”) and ends with his promise of the mountains dropping new wine, so Joel's book was finished before Amos gathered his. Driver reports that Credner placed Joel in Joash's early reign, when the priest Jehoiada led and no king is named, and that “most scholars until recently acquiesced in his conclusion”. Amos 1:2 Joel 3:16 [8][1][7]
After the exile, in the Persian period
S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1898)

Driver: Joel names no king, no Assyria or Babylon, and no northern kingdom, and speaks of Israel “scattered among the nations”; these features “turn the balance of evidence somewhat strongly in favour of the later date”. Smith places him among the prophets of the Persian period, “writing towards 400 B.C.”. Joel 3:2 [1][7]
Kessner (1888), as reported by G. A. Smith (1898)
Smith notes that Kessner “deems the date unprovable”; Driver too says the date depends “entirely upon internal evidence”.[7][1]
The book names no king and gives no date.
Scripture does not say where Joel lived, though his words centre on Zion and the house of the LORD.
Scripture does not record Joel's death; no tradition of it was found in the sources read.
